title: IBM Links Two Nighthawk r3 Chips To Make A 1,040-Qubit Quantum System
author: Jeff Burt
text:
COMPUTE

IBM Links Two Nighthawk r3 Chips To Make A 1,040-Qubit Quantum System

Jeff Burt

Jeff
Burt

Published
tue 17 Nov 2026 // 17:13 UTC

Big Blue has been on a tear for the past couple of years detailing the strides it’s making towards meeting its ambitious goal of launching a fault-tolerant quantum computer in 2029, highlighting progress in a range of areas, from error correction and quantum advantage to more tightly tying together quantum and classical HPC computing.A year ago this month, IBM announced Nighthawk (below), a follow-on to its Heron quantum processor that includes 120 qubits and its square-lattice architecture, a shift in topology away from its earlier heavy-hex technology that brings greater qubit connectivity, crosstalk management, and circuit depth performance. In September, IBM unveiled Nighthawk r2, another 120-qubit QPU that comes with a new reset system that pushes throughput up to more than 100,000 circuits per second.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

In the meantime, research papers have outlined three demonstrations of quantum advantage run on IBM’s Heron quantum chips and the unveiling of a modular and scalable cryogenic cooling system that will be critical to its plans for the fault-tolerant Starling system in 2029 and another example of the company’s modular approach to quantum infrastructure.

The also were announcements about achievements made with partners, including AMD and Oak Ridge National Laboratory in quantum-classical computing error correction and the RIKEN Institute in Japan and the Cleveland Clinic about the work that can be done now with hybrid quantum and classical computing in scientific research.This week, at the IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 in Chicago, the company outlined advancements in speed and quality the Nighthawk r2 QPUs are making and plans to run out Nighthawk r3, its next-generation quantum chip, in 2027. The company also plans to release a device that will use long-range couplers (l-couplers) to join together two Nighthawk r3 processors into a single system.

IBM executives said that when talking about quantum workloads, speed is just as important as scale and quality, noting that more applications are requiring circuits that can execute thousands of operations on 100 qubits or more to generation millions to billions of samples. Quantum systems will need to see jumps in speed to ensure such applications can be run fast enough and at acceptable costs.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

The design for Nighthawk r2 is already making strides in that direction, according to Oliver Dial, IBM Fellow and the vendor’s senior vice president of quantum systems. As with the first Nighthawk iteration, r2 includes 120 qubits, but it also comes with on-chip qubit reset, Dial told journalists during a briefing before the event.

“This is an extra physical qubit that we glued on the chip for each programmable qubit that lets us quickly remove the energy from one of our programmable qubits, returning it to the ground state,” he said. “That capability lets our users run circuits on this chip faster than was ever before possible. In fact, in the first three weeks that this device was available, our users ran 8 billion circuits on it.”Since September, more than 34 billion circuits have run on Nighthawk r2, and IBM has run 7,500 gates on the chip, 19 times faster than it would have taken for Nighthawk r1 due to the reset capability.Nighthawk r3 will scale to more 520 qubits and support 10,000 quantum operations and, while retaining the square-lattice connectivity, will include 10 chip-to-chip l-coupler interconnects that can be used for larger quantum systems. Connecting two Nighthawk r3 processors will create a 1,040-qubit system that can run larger and more complex computations.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Nighthawk r3 will be manufactured at the Anderon 300-millimeter quantum superconducting wafer foundry in Albany, New York. (Below) Anderon is an IBM subsidiary that expanded its operations after the US Commerce Department in May contributed $1 billion through the federal CHIPS Act. IBM contributed a $1 billion investment of its own. As a side note, Global Foundries also received $375 million from the Commerce Department to develop a quantum foundry.

The l-couplers are key to performance and scalability improvements, Dial said. IBM connected Nighthawk r1 processors using four l-couplers and reaching 99.3 percent quantum state transfer fidelity, closing in on the company’s goal of 99.9 percent.“And cooling down right now in Poughkeepsie, New York [home of IBM’s Quantum Data Center] is a first, joining two processors in two different refrigerators with four l-couplers, only this time is Nighthawk r2s,” Dial said. “We think that this progress shows that we are well advanced on our path towards building Starling.”

Starling is expected to be the fault-tolerant system that arrives in 2029, with 200 logical qubits capable of running 100 million quantum operations. A key for IBM with Starling is the planned use of bivariate bicycle codes, a class of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) error correction codes that reduce the number of physical qubits needed to make up logical qubits and the quantum information they hold.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Starling’s successor, Blue Jay, will come in 2033 or later.

“A lot of the technologies that we're premiering in Nighthawk are also going to help us build Starling,” he said. “Our path to large-scale fault tolerance is the only practical approach to fault tolerance out there. That's because it's built on a universal Pauli-based computation architecture that uses an error-correcting code that’s over 10x more efficient than alternatives [like surface codes]. It's built on a modular platform, which lets us build modules that are the same size and complexity as what we're already capable of building today and join them together to build this enormous platform.”Dial added: “It's that modularity and the efficiency of this design that's really key to the practicality. There are several key technologies that we need to demonstrate in order to bring this architecture to reality. This includes device physics for higher connectivity – c-couplers – packaging for more signals, decoders, the ability to detect and correct a computation for the presence of errors, modular QPUs with l-couplers, as mentioned before for Nighthawk R3, a modular cryogenic system, and modular control electronics.”Asked what other milestones need to be reached for starling, Dial pointed to “bigger, better devices,” “more wiring,” the capability to demonstrate the modular cryogenic cooling system at a scale about three times more than what they can do today, and the ability to run decoding in real time.IBM also continues to push the tighter alignment of quantum systems with classical computers. The latest step introduced at the event this week is IBM bringing classical HPC computing and quantum into a single managed environment on IBM’s Quantum Platform, which will allow organizations to integrate quantum workflows with a classical compute, ranging from laptops to supercomputers, or with classical resources now available on the platform.It dovetails with IBM’s announcement this month of a co-design platform for error correction that brought together Big Blue’s Nighthawk r2 and Oak Ridge’s Umbra supercomputer – powered by AMD Epyc datacenter chips and Instinct GPUs – in the same datacenter in Poughkeepsie, New York.The managed offering “allows you to provision for a class of compute, ranging in different sizes of compute, from CPU-based all the way up to GPU-based, and have it in the same environment in which you are running your quantum computer execution,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric supercomputing. “You can have persistence across the jobs that you want to run, as well as a simple way to pay for both the classical and quantum resources in one place.”
